en: Mahāniddesa,
Aṭṭhakavagga, 7. Tissa-metteyya-sutta-niddesa (The Exposition of the Discourse to Tissa-metteyya)
Now he will explain the exposition of the Tissa-Metteyya Sutta:
"For one devoted to sexual intercourse," said the Venerable Tissa Metteyya.
Tell us of obstacles, O venerable sir;
having heard your instruction,
we shall train ourselves in solitude.
"Engaged in sexual intercourse":

what is called "the nature of sexual intercourse" (methunadhamma)? It is that which is contrary to the true Dhamma, the village custom, the practice of the low-born, the vile, the water-rite, the secret, the mutual attainment of the couple.
For what reason is it called the nature of sexual intercourse?
Because it is a common practice for both who are lustful, infatuated, lecherous, obsessed, and whose minds are overwhelmed— to engage in it,
it is therefore called the “practice of sexual intercourse.
Just as two who create strife are called “quarrelers,” and two who create disputes are called “quarrelers,” so too is this called the “practice of sexual intercourse.”
Both those who engage in talk are called "those engaged in sexual intercourse"; both those who engage in disputes are called "those engaged in sexual intercourse";

both those who engage in legal issues are called "those engaged in sexual intercourse"; both those who are disputants are called "those engaged in sexual intercourse"; both those who engage in debate are called "those engaged in sexual intercourse."
In the same way, for both who are lustful, inflamed with passion, lecherous, obsessed, and whose minds are overwhelmed— for both who are alike in this respect—
it is called "the practice of sexual intercourse" (*methunadhamma*) because it is a common activity.
Thus, "one intent upon sexual intercourse."

"One who is engaged in, intent upon, devoted to, fully committed to, practicing, habituated to, regarding as important, inclined toward, leaning toward, bent toward, dedicated to, and dominated by sexual intercourse"—
this refers to one who is addicted to sexual intercourse.
Thus spoke the Venerable Tissa Metteyya.

"Thus" (iccāti) means: the conjunction of words, the connection of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of consonants, and the sequential order of words—this is "thus.
"Venerable sir" (āyasmāti) means: a term of endearment, a term of respect, a term of reverence, and a term of deference—this is "venerable sir."
"Venerable sir":
"Tissa" is the name, designation, appellation, usage, name, naming, denomination, expression, phrasing, and utterance of that elder.
"Metteyya" is the clan, designation, appellation, and usage of that elder.
"Thus spoke the venerable Tissa Metteyya:
'Speak of affliction, dear sir. 'Affliction' means:
speak of, declare, show, describe, point out, establish, set forth, reveal, analyze, make plain, and explain affliction, injury, oppression, friction, calamity, and misfortune."
“Mārisa” is a term of endearment, a term of respect, a term of reverence, a term of deference;
“Mārisa, speak of the affliction;
having heard your instruction,” [he said].
"Having heard, having listened to, having grasped, having retained, having reflected upon, and having discerned your word, your manner of speech, your teaching, your instruction, and your guidance"—
this is what is meant by "having heard your message.
"We shall train ourselves in seclusion."
There are these three kinds of seclusion:
seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from acquisitions.
What is seclusion of body?

Here, a bhikkhu resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw. He dwells physically secluded.
He goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, enters the village alone for alms, returns alone, sits alone in private, undertakes walking meditation alone, and wanders alone.
He dwells alone; he moves, conducts himself, maintains himself, preserves himself, and sustains himself—this is physical seclusion.
What is mental seclusion?
The mind of one who has attained the first jhāna is secluded from the hindrances;
the mind of one who has attained the second jhāna is secluded from applied and sustained thought;
the mind of one who has attained the third jhāna is secluded from rapture.
The mind of one who has attained the fourth jhāna is secluded from pleasure and pain;
the mind of one who has attained the base of infinite space is secluded from perceptions of form, perceptions of sensory impact, and perceptions of diversity;
the mind of one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness is secluded from the perception of the base of infinite space.
The mind of one who has attained the base of nothingness is secluded from the perception of the base of infinite consciousness;
the mind of one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is secluded from the perception of the base of nothingness;

and the mind of a stream-enterer is secluded from personality-belief, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the defilements associated with them.

The mind of a once-returner is secluded from the gross fetters of sensual lust and ill will, from the gross underlying tendencies of sensual lust and ill will, and from the defilements associated with them;

the mind of a non-returner is secluded from the residual fetters of sensual lust and ill will, from the residual underlying tendencies of sensual lust and ill will, and from the defilements associated with them.

For an Arahant, the mind is secluded from attachment to the form realm, attachment to the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to attachment to existence, the underlying tendency to ignorance, and from the defilements associated with these, as well as from all external signs—
this is seclusion of mind. What is seclusion of acquisitions?
"Bases" (upadhi) are said to be the defilements, the aggregates, and volitional formations.
"Seclusion from bases" (upadhiviveka) is said to be the deathless Nibbāna—
that which is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all bases, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna.
This is seclusion from acquisitions.
There is physical seclusion for those who have withdrawn their bodies and delight in renunciation;
and there is mental seclusion for those whose minds are purified and who have attained supreme clarity.
"And there is seclusion from acquisitions for those persons who are without acquisitions and have reached the cessation of formations.
'We shall train in seclusion,' [he thinks].
That elder was by nature one who had trained in the training."
Moreover, referring to the teaching of the Dhamma, while encouraging the teaching of the Dhamma, he said:
"We shall train ourselves in seclusion.
Therefore, the elder Tissa Metteyya said:
“Tell me, dear sir, of the distress for one who is devoted to sexual intercourse,” said the Venerable Tissa Metteyya.
"Having heard your teaching,
we shall train ourselves in seclusion.
[But] for one devoted to sexual intercourse...
"Metteyya," said the Blessed One,
"or else he will cause the teaching to perish,
and he will practice wrongly."
This is what is ignoble in that regard.
Regarding "one intent on sexual intercourse":
sexual intercourse means that which is contrary to the true Dhamma, the village custom, the practice of the low-born, the vile, the water-rite, the secret, the mutual attainment of the couple.
For what reason is it called the practice of sexual intercourse?
Because it is a common practice for two people who are lustful, infatuated, lecherous, obsessed, and whose minds are overwhelmed— two who are similar—
it is for that reason called the practice of sexual intercourse.

Just as both quarrelsome ones are called "a pair," both contentious ones are called "a pair," both disputatious ones are called "a pair," both wrangling ones are called "a pair," both litigants are called "a pair," both debaters are called "a pair," and both those who engage in discussion...
They are called "those engaged in sexual intercourse.
In the same way, because it is a common practice for both who are lustful, inflamed with passion, lecherous, obsessed, and whose minds are overwhelmed—
therefore it is called "the practice of sexual intercourse" (*methunadhamma*).

"Engaged in sexual intercourse": one who is engaged in, intent upon, devoted to, fully occupied with, habitually practicing, frequently practicing, making it a heavy burden, inclined toward, prone toward, leaning toward, intent upon, and dominated by the practice of sexual intercourse—
this is "one engaged in sexual intercourse."
"Metteyya"—the Blessed One addresses that elder by his clan name.
"Bhagavā" is a term signifying reverence;
moreover, he is called "Bhagavā" because he has destroyed passion (*bhagga-rāgo*).
The Blessed One has destroyed the defects;
the Blessed One has destroyed delusion;
the Blessed One has destroyed conceit.
The Blessed One has destroyed wrong views;
the Blessed One has destroyed thorns;
the Blessed One has destroyed the defilements.
The Blessed One has enjoyed, distributed, and shared the jewel of the Dhamma;
the Blessed One makes an end of existence;
the Blessed One is one who has cultivated the body, cultivated virtue, cultivated the mind, and cultivated wisdom.
The Blessed One frequented remote lodgings in forest and jungle tracts—places with little sound, little noise, secluded from people, hidden from the crowd, and suitable for seclusion;
thus he is the Blessed One. Or, the Blessed One is a partaker of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; thus he is the Blessed One.
Or, the Blessed One is a partaker of the flavor of meaning, the flavor of the Dhamma, the flavor of liberation, of higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom; thus he is the Blessed One.
The Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the four jhānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments;
or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, and the nine successive dwellings in attainment;
or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the ten developments of perception, the ten kasiṇa attainments, the concentration of mindfulness of breathing, and the attainment of the foul.

The Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right endeavors, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path;

or the Blessed One is "Bhagavā" because he possesses the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the six direct knowledges, and the six qualities of a Buddha.

"Bhagavā" is not a name given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister, nor by friends and companions, nor by kinsmen and blood relations, nor by recluses and brahmins, nor by deities.
This is a designation based on liberation, realized at the foot of the Bodhi tree upon the attainment of omniscient knowledge by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; that is to say, "Bhagavā."
"Metteyya," said the Blessed One.
"Or the Dispensation may be forgotten. The Dispensation is forgotten for two reasons: [the first is]... [the second is]... [text continues].
The teaching of the scriptures is forgotten, and the teaching of practice is forgotten.
What is the teaching of the scriptures?
That which has been mastered by him.

The discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), "thus-it-was-said" sayings (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma),
and analytical expositions (vedalla)— this is the teaching of the scriptures (pariyatti-sāsana). That too is forgotten, utterly forgotten, lost, completely lost, and becomes externalized.
In this way too, the teaching may be forgotten.
What is the teaching of practice?
It is the right practice, the conformable practice, the non-adversarial practice, the practice according to the goal, and the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
Complete fulfillment of the moral precepts, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness,
mindfulness and clear comprehension, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five spiritual faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
This is the teaching of practice (*paṭipatti-sāsana*).
That too may be forgotten, utterly forgotten, lost, completely lost, and become externalized.
Thus, the teaching may also be forgotten.
"And he practices wrongly" means: he kills living beings,
takes what is not given, breaks into dwellings, commits robbery, commits burglary, lies in wait on highways, commits adultery with another's wife, and speaks falsehoods—
it is in this way that he practices wrongly.
“This is un-Aryan in him”: this un-Aryan quality,
this quality of a fool, a deluded quality, a quality of ignorance, a quality of the “ocean of dispute,” namely wrong practice—
this is what is un-Aryan in that person.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“To one devoted to sexual intercourse,” (said the Blessed One, “O Metteyya”).
Or even if you must uphold the Teaching,
yet you practice wrongly—
this in him is what is un-Aryan.
He who, having formerly practiced alone,
now indulges in sexual intercourse,
is like a wandering carriage in this world.
"They call the worldling inferior.
"Having practiced alone in the past"—
this is said for two reasons regarding one who has practiced alone in the past.
Either by way of what is termed "going forth" (pabbajjā) or by way of the sense of "releasing from the crowd" (gaṇāvavassagga).
How [is it] by way of what is termed "going forth"?
Having previously wandered alone, having cut off all the impediments of household life, having cut off the impediment of wife and children, and having cut off the impediment of relatives...
Having severed the impediment of friends and companions, having severed the impediment of stored-up possessions,
having shaved off his hair and beard, having donned saffron-colored robes, and having gone forth from the home life into homelessness,
he has attained the state of owning nothing; he wanders alone, dwells alone, moves, conducts himself, maintains, preserves, and sustains himself.
Thus, having previously wandered alone under the designation of "going forth," how did he previously wander alone for the sake of release from the crowd?
Having thus gone forth, he dwells alone in remote forest dwellings and jungle-thickets— lodgings that are quiet, noiseless, secluded from people, private from men, and suitable for retreat.
Thus, he goes alone, stands alone, sits alone, lies down alone, enters the village for alms alone,
returns alone, sits in private alone, and resolves upon the walking meditation alone;
he wanders, dwells, moves, conducts himself, protects, maintains, and sustains himself alone.
Thus, having previously wandered alone for the sake of avoiding the company of others,
he who indulges in sexual intercourse—
this is what is called "sexual misconduct" (*methunadhamma*), which is that which is not the true Dhamma... [and so forth].
For that reason, it is called the practice of sexual intercourse.
"One who indulges in sexual intercourse":

one who, at a later time, having renounced the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, has returned to the low life and indulges in, engages in, practices, and pursues the practice of sexual intercourse.
He who indulges in sexual intercourse wanders about like one in a vehicle. "Vehicle" refers to an elephant-vehicle,
a horse-vehicle, a cow-vehicle, a goat-vehicle, a ram-vehicle, a camel-vehicle, or a donkey-vehicle— wandering about in such a vehicle.
An unbroken, untamed, and undisciplined horse goes off the path, climbs over uneven stumps and rocks,
breaks the carriage or its harness, and even falls down a precipice—
just as such a wild carriage, being unbroken, untamed, and undisciplined, goes off the path.
In the same way, that renegade who resembles a wandering carriage takes to the wrong path, adopts wrong view... [and so on] ...adopts wrong concentration.
Just as a wandering carriage that is untamed, untrained, undisciplined, and uneven mounts over stumps and rocks;
even so, that renegade who resembles a wandering carriage mounts upon uneven bodily action, uneven...
He ascends to unrighteousness of verbal action; he ascends to unrighteousness of mental action; he ascends to unrighteous killing;
he ascends to unrighteous taking of what is not given; he ascends to unrighteous sexual misconduct;
he ascends to unrighteous false speech; he ascends to unrighteous divisive speech; he ascends to unrighteous harsh speech; he ascends to unrighteous...
One mounts upon idle chatter; one mounts upon unwholesome covetousness; one mounts upon unwholesome ill will;
one mounts upon unwholesome wrong view; one mounts upon unwholesome volitional formations; one mounts upon the unwholesome five strands of sensual pleasure;
one mounts upon the unwholesome hindrances.
Just as an unbroken, untamed, untrained, and undisciplined carriage breaks both the vehicle and the rider,
even so that run-away monk, resembling an unbroken carriage, destroys himself in hell, destroys himself in the animal realm,
destroys himself in the sphere of hungry ghosts, destroys himself in the human world, and destroys himself in the world of the devas.
Just as that wandering vehicle— unbroken, unmade, untamed, and undisciplined— falls over a precipice,
even so does that wanderer, resembling a wandering vehicle, fall over the precipice of birth, fall over the precipice of aging,
fall over the precipice of illness, fall over the precipice of death, and fall over the precipice of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
"In the world"— that is, in the world of the lower realms and the world of humans—
that world is like a wandering vehicle;
they call the worldling "inferior."
In what sense are they called "puthujjana"?
They are called *puthujjana* because they generate various (*puthu*) defilements; they are called *puthujjana* because they have not abandoned the various views of identity (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*);
they are called *puthujjana* because they look toward the faces of various teachers; they are called *puthujjana* because they have not emerged from the various realms of existence (*gati*).

They are called *puthujjana* because they perform various and manifold volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*); they are called *puthujjana* because they are carried away by various and manifold floods (*ogha*);

they are called *puthujjana* because they are tormented by various and manifold fevers (*santāpa*); they are called *puthujjana* because they are consumed by various and manifold burning pains (*pariḷāha*);
and they are called *puthujjana* because they are attached, greedy, infatuated, maddened, obsessed, and stuck to the fivefold strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*) individually.

"Ordinary persons (puthujjana) are those who are stuck and obstructed; ordinary persons are those who are individually shut in, covered, enveloped, blocked, concealed, and closed off by the five hindrances.
They are called 'ordinary' because they are base."

"They say of the worldling that he is inferior, base, low, wretched, a mere fourfold [group], and limited; thus they speak, thus they discourse, thus they utter, thus they illuminate, thus they designate him"—thus they call the worldling "inferior.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“He who, having previously lived alone,
now indulges in sexual intercourse,
is like a wandering vehicle in this world.”
They call the worldling base.
Whatever fame and renown he previously had,
that too diminishes for him.
Seeing this as well,
one should train to abandon sexual intercourse;
even that fame and reputation one had before may diminish for such a person.

What is fame? Here, someone was previously honored, revered, esteemed, worshiped, and venerated while still in the state of a recluse, and was a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick—
this is fame.
What is fame?

Here, someone in his former state as a recluse has attained a reputation for praise: he is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, a brilliant speaker, and possessed of eloquence—whether as a master of the Suttas, a keeper of the Vinaya, an expounder of the Dhamma, a forest-dweller, or an alms-collector.
Whether he is a wearer of rag-robes, or a wearer of the three robes, or one who goes on a continuous alms-round, or one who eats only from a single bowl, or one who remains in a sitting posture,
or one who accepts whatever seat is offered,
or one who has attained the first jhāna, or one who has attained the second jhāna, or one who has attained the third jhāna.
Or whether one is an attainer of the fourth jhāna, or an attainer of the attainment of the base of infinite space, or an attainer of the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness,
or an attainer of the attainment of the base of nothingness, or an attainer of the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
this is "renown."
Whatever fame and reputation he previously had,

that too diminishes for him. Later on, having renounced the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, and having returned to the lower life, that fame and reputation of his diminishes, wanes, fades away, falls off, disappears, and is utterly destroyed.
"And that fame and reputation which he previously had may even diminish for him. Having seen this as well, one should train thus: "Sexual intercourse must be abandoned.

Here, "this" refers to the fame and reputation he previously had during his state as a recluse, and later, upon renouncing the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, the infamy and lack of reputation of one who has returned to the lower life.
"Having seen this success and failure" means:
having seen, weighed, scrutinized, discerned, and made manifest;
thus, "having seen" this as well.
"One should train" refers to the three trainings:
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom.
What is the training in higher virtue?

Here, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
There is the minor aggregate of virtue and the major aggregate of virtue.
Virtue is the foundation, the beginning, the footings, the restraint, the control, the gateway, and the primary means for the attainment of wholesome states.
This is the training in higher virtue.
What is the training in higher mind?

Here, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion …pe…
He enters and dwells in the second jhāna… the third jhāna… the fourth jhāna.
This is the training in higher mind.
What is the training in higher wisdom?
Here, a bhikkhu is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
Thus one understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; one understands as it really is:

"This is the origin of suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; one understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. One understands as it really is: "These are the taints";

one understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; one understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints"; one understands as it really is: "This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints."
This is the training in higher wisdom.
What is called "sexual intercourse" is that which is contrary to the true Dhamma...
for that reason it is called sexual intercourse.
"Having seen this too, one should train thus: 'Sexual intercourse is to be abandoned.

For the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, and the calming of sexual intercourse, one should train in the higher virtue (*adhisīla*), one should train in the higher mind (*adhicitta*), and one should train in the higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*).
One should train while attending to these three trainings; one should train knowing them, one should train seeing them, and one should train reflecting upon them.
One should train; resolving with the mind, one should train; resolving with faith, one should train; exerting energy, one should train;
establishing mindfulness, one should train; concentrating the mind, one should train;
understanding with wisdom, one should train; directly knowing what is to be directly known, one should train; fully understanding what is to be fully understood, one should train.

One should train; training while abandoning what is to be abandoned, training while developing what is to be developed, training while realizing what is to be realized—one should practice, practice thoroughly, and conduct oneself by undertaking [the training].
Seeing this, one should train thus: "Sexual intercourse is to be utterly abandoned."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“The fame and reputation one had before may now diminish for that person.”
"Seeing this too, one should train to abandon sexual intercourse.
Thus he was overcome by his own thoughts.
He broods like one who is wretched;
having heard the reproach of others,
such a person becomes dejected.
"Ensnared by his intentions, he broods like a pauper.
Struck, ensnared, overcome, possessed, covered by the intention for sensual desire, the intention for ill will, the intention for cruelty,
and the intention for wrong view, he broods, broods deeply, like a pauper, like one who is dull-witted, like one who is utterly deluded.
He meditates, premeditates, out-meditates, and inter-meditates.
Just as an owl, seeking a mouse on a tree branch, meditates, premeditates, out-meditates, and inter-meditates;
just as a jackal, seeking fish on a riverbank, meditates, premeditates, out-meditates, and inter-meditates.
Just as a cat, seeking a mouse in a cramped, dusty corner at a junction, broods, broods deeply, broods intensely,
and broods excessively; just as a donkey, having broken its harness, broods, broods deeply, broods intensely,
and broods excessively in a cramped, dusty corner at a junction;
In the same way, that wanderer— touched, overcome, deluded, possessed, enveloped, and impoverished by thoughts of sensual desire,
ill will, cruelty, and wrong views— meditates, meditates deeply, meditates intensely, and meditates excessively, like one who is dull, feeble, and utterly bewildered.
"Oppressed by his own thoughts, he broods like a beggar.
Hearing the reproach of others, such a person becomes dejected. Regarding "the reproach of others":
it means that preceptors, teachers, fellow disciples, fellow students, friends, those seen together, those who have shared a meal, or companions reprove him.
“Friend, it is a loss for you, it is a misfortune for you, that having obtained such a sublime Teacher,
having gone forth in such a well-proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya, and having obtained such a noble assembly, you have—
on account of the base act of sexual intercourse— renounced the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, and returned to the lower life.”
"Indeed, you had no faith in wholesome states; indeed, you had no sense of shame in wholesome states;
indeed, you had no fear of wrongdoing in wholesome states; indeed, you had no energy in wholesome states;
indeed, you had no mindfulness in wholesome states; indeed, you had no wisdom in wholesome states."

Having heard, listened to, mastered, retained, reflected upon, and discerned their words, their manner of speech, their teaching, their instruction, and their guidance, he becomes dejected; he is oppressed, struck, afflicted, and miserable.
"Of such a kind" means of such a kind, of that sort, established in that way, of that character, and of that appearance.
He who is a deserter—this is what is meant.
Having heard the reproach of others, such a person becomes dejected.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"He is overcome by his own thoughts..."
He broods like one who is miserable;
having heard the reproach of others,
such a person becomes dejected.
If, being provoked by the arguments of opponents,
one engages in disputes, this indeed is his great snare.
"He plunges into what is censurable;
then he engages in disputes, being provoked by the arguments of others.

Here, "then" (*atha*) refers to the connection of words, the conjunction of words, the completion of the phrase, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of the consonants, and the sequential order of the words.
Now, as for "weapons": there are three weapons— the weapon of the body,
the weapon of speech, and the weapon of the mind.
The threefold misconduct of body is the weapon of the body; the fourfold misconduct of speech is the weapon of speech; the threefold misconduct of mind is the weapon of the mind.
"Charged by others' doctrines" means:

being charged by preceptors, or teachers, or those with the same preceptor, or those with the same teacher, or by friends, or those seen together, or intimates, or companions, he speaks a deliberate lie.
“I was delighted, Bhante, with the going forth.
I have returned because my mother must be supported,” he said.
“I have returned because my father must be supported,” he said.
“My brother must be supported… my sister must be supported… my son must be supported…”
My daughter must be supported… my friends must be supported… my ministers must be supported…
"My relatives must be supported...
my blood relations must be supported; for that reason I have left the order"—thus he speaks.
He wields the weapon of speech; he mingles it, generates it, produces it, brings it forth, and fully manifests it.
Then, being challenged by the doctrines of others, he fabricates arguments.
This indeed is his great obsession.

This is his great obsession: this deliberate lying is a great forest, a great thicket, a great wilderness, a great unevenness, a great crookedness, a great mire, a great quagmire, a great impediment, and a great bond.
This, indeed, is his great snare:
he strikes at false speech.
"False speech" is said to be lying.
Here, someone, having been summoned as a witness and questioned in an assembly, or in a gathering, or in the midst of kinsmen, or in the midst of a guild, or in the royal court—
"Come now, good man, speak what you know"—
if he does not know, he says, "I know."
Knowing, one says, “I do not know”;
not seeing, one says, “I see”;
or seeing, one says, “I do not see.”
Thus, one who speaks a deliberate lie for one's own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some trifling material gain—
this is called the transgression of lying. Furthermore,
there are three ways in which false speech occurs.
Before speaking, he thinks:
"I will speak falsely"; while speaking, he thinks:
"I am speaking falsely"; after having spoken, he thinks: [“I have spoken falsely”].
“I spoke falsely.
In these three ways, there is false speech.
Furthermore, there is false speech in four ways.
Before speaking, he thinks:
"I will speak falsely"; while speaking, he thinks:
"I am speaking falsely"; after having spoken, he thinks: [“I have spoken falsely.”]
“I spoke falsely,” having set aside one’s own view.
In these four ways there is false speech.
Furthermore, there are five ways…
False speech occurs in six ways … in seven ways … in eight ways.
Before he speaks, the thought occurs to him:
"I shall speak a falsehood"; while speaking, it occurs to him:
"I am speaking a falsehood"; and after having spoken, it occurs to him: [“I have spoken a falsehood.”]
“I said what was false,” having set aside one’s view, having set aside one’s preference, having set aside one’s inclination, having set aside one’s perception, and having set aside one’s disposition.
In these eight ways there is false speech.
Thus one plunges into the offense of lying.
"He plunges into, enters into, immerses himself in, and penetrates the offense of lying"—
thus he "plunges into the offense of lying.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“When, being challenged by the doctrines of others,
one engages in disputes, this indeed is his great snare.”
He plunges into what is blameworthy.
Though renowned as "wise," he is intent upon living alone.
And even though he is engaged in sexual intercourse,
he wallows like a fool;
yet he is known by the designation "wise man."
In this case, someone, while formerly in the state of being a recluse, had acquired a reputation for praise:
"He is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, eloquent, and possessed of ready wit; he is a master of the Suttas, or a keeper of the Vinaya, or a preacher of the Dhamma...
[and so on] ...or one who has attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Thus he is known, recognized, and designated;
he is designated as "wise.
He is resolute in a certain teacher.
One is intent upon living alone for two reasons:
either by way of what is termed "going forth" or by way of the sense of seclusion from the group.
How is one intent upon living alone by way of what is termed "going forth"?
Having severed all the impediments of household life...
[as above] ...thus he is resolved upon the solitary life, which is designated as "going forth.
How is he resolved upon the solitary life in the sense of release from the crowd?
Having thus gone forth, he dwells alone in remote forest thickets and jungle retreats... Thus,
in the sense of relinquishing the company [of others], he is resolved upon the solitary life— thus he is "resolved upon the solitary life."
"And he is engaged in sexual intercourse.
Sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*) is that which is contrary to the true Dhamma, the village custom... [etc.
...for that reason it is called sexual intercourse.
"And he is engaged in sexual intercourse":

at a later time, having renounced the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, and having returned to the lower life, he is engaged in, intent upon, devoted to, and occupied with the practice of sexual intercourse—
thus, "he is engaged in sexual intercourse."
"He wallows about like a fool":
like one who is wretched, like one who is dull-witted, like one who is utterly deluded, he wallows, wallows about, and becomes defiled.
He kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, commits robbery, acts as a housebreaker, lies in ambush, commits adultery, and speaks falsehoods.
In this way, he is tormented, thoroughly tormented, and utterly defiled.
Kings seize him and subject him to various punishments—
they beat him with whips, they beat him with canes, they beat him with clubs, and they cut off his hands.
They cut off a foot; they cut off both hands and feet; they cut off an ear; they cut off a nose; they cut off both ears and nose;
they make them undergo the *bilaṅgathālika* torture; they make them undergo the *saṅkhamuṇḍika* torture;

they make them undergo the *rāhumukha* torture; they make them undergo the *jotimālika* torture; they make them undergo the *hatthapajjotika* torture; they make them undergo the *erakavattika* torture.
They make them wear garments of bark; they make them wear the skin of an antelope; they make them wear a string of fish-hooks; they make them wear a string of coins;
they make them undergo the punishment of being scraped with salt; they make them undergo the punishment of being turned over a crossbar;
they make them sit on a chair of straw; they douse them with boiling oil; they have them devoured by dogs; and while still alive, they impale them on stakes.
They even cut off one’s head with a sword.
In this way too, one is tormented, thoroughly tormented, and utterly defiled.
Or else, overcome by the craving for sensual pleasures and with mind consumed by them, one seeks wealth upon the great ocean by boat.
He leaps forward, preceded by cold and preceded by heat; oppressed by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things,
and tormented by hunger and thirst, he goes to Tigumba, he goes to Takkola,
he goes to Takkasilā, he goes to Kālamukha, he goes to Purapura, he goes to Vesuṅga, he goes to Verāpatha.

He goes; he goes swiftly; he goes to Tāmali, he goes to Vaṅga, he goes to Eḷabandhana, he goes to Suvaṇṇakūṭa, he goes to Suvaṇṇabhūmi, he goes to Tambapaṇṇi, he goes to Suppāraka, he goes to Bhārukaccha, he goes to Suratta, he goes to Bhaṅgaloka, he goes to Bhaṅgaṇa.
He goes along a most broken path; he goes along a path of wombs, he goes along a supreme womb-path, he goes along a path of withered grass,
he goes along a path of roots, he goes along a desert wilderness, he goes along a path for knees, he goes along a path for goats, he goes along a path for rams,
he goes along a path of spikes, he goes along a path of umbrellas, he goes along a path of bamboo.
He goes along the path of birds, he goes along the path of mice, he goes along the path of wild beasts, he goes along the path of thorns.
In this way too, he is worn out, thoroughly worn out, and utterly defiled.
Seeking, he does not find; he experiences pain and mental distress rooted in failure to obtain.
In this way, one is harassed, tormented, and defiled.
While seeking, one finds; and having found, one experiences suffering and grief rooted in the need for protection, thinking:
"How can it be that kings do not seize my wealth, thieves do not seize it, fire does not burn it, water does not carry it away, and unpleasant heirs do not take it?"
While he is thus guarding and protecting them, those possessions go to ruin.
He experiences suffering and mental distress rooted in that loss.
In this way, too, he is worn out, utterly worn out, and completely defiled.
And he, though engaged in sexual intercourse, wallows like a fool.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"One who is designated as 'wise'..."
Though he is resolved upon the solitary life,
if he is still intent on sexual intercourse,
he will wallow like a dullard.
Having understood this danger here,
both in the past and the future,
the sage should make firm his solitary wandering.
"One should not indulge in sexual intercourse.
Having understood this danger—both here and in the past and future—the sage [acts thus].

Here, "this" refers to the fame and reputation one had previously in the state of being a recluse, as well as the infamy and lack of reputation for one who, at a later time, having renounced the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the training, returns to the lower life.
"Having known this success and failure"—
that is, having understood, weighed, scrutinized, discerned, and made manifest. "The Sage" (muni).
"Mona" is said to be knowledge.
That which is wisdom, understanding... [and so on] ...having transcended the net of attachments, he is a sage (*muni*).
"Here" means in this view, in this inclination, in this preference, in this adoption, in this Dhamma.
"In this discipline, in this Dhamma-discipline, in this teaching, in this holy life,
in this instruction of the Teacher, in this personal existence, in this human world"—
having understood this danger regarding what precedes and what follows here, the sage [remains detached].
"One should make a firm practice of living alone.
One should make a firm practice of living alone for two reasons:
either by way of what is termed "going forth" or by way of the sense of relief from the crowd.
How should one make firm the practice of solitary wandering,
which is designated as "going forth"? Having severed all the impediments of household life, having severed the impediment of children and wife, having severed the impediment of relatives,
having severed the impediment of friends and companions, and having severed the impediment of hoarding, [one should shave off] the hair and beard...
Having cast off the marks of a householder, having donned saffron robes, and having gone forth from the home life into homelessness,
one should attain the state of possessing nothing and should wander, dwell, conduct oneself, behave, protect oneself, maintain oneself, and sustain oneself alone. In this way,
by means of what is termed "going forth," one should make firm the practice of solitary wandering.
How should one make the solitary life firm by means of release from the crowd?

Having thus gone forth, he should resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats—places that are quiet, free from noise, secluded from people, private from men, and suitable for seclusion.
He should go alone, stand alone, sit alone, lie down alone, and enter the village alone for alms.
One should enter alone, one should go back alone, one should sit in seclusion alone, one should undertake the walking meditation alone;
one should wander, dwell, conduct oneself, behave, preserve oneself, maintain oneself, and sustain oneself alone.
Thus, by way of relinquishing the group, one should make the solitary life firm.

One should make one’s solitary wandering firm; one should make it steadfast; one should be firmly committed and resolutely dedicated to wholesome states—thus, "one should make one’s solitary wandering firm.
One should not indulge in sexual intercourse.
“Sexual intercourse” means that which is contrary to the true Dhamma, the village custom...
[and so on] ...for that reason it is called sexual intercourse.

“One should not engage in sexual intercourse” means one should not practice it, should not pursue it, should not indulge in it, should not resort to it, should not perform it, should not practice it habitually, and should not live having undertaken it.
One should not indulge in sexual intercourse.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Having understood this danger..."
A sage here, regarding what precedes and what follows,
should make firm his practice of solitude and not indulge in sexual intercourse.
One should train in discernment alone;
this is the supreme quality of the noble ones.
One should not, on account of it, consider oneself superior.
"He is indeed close to Nibbāna.
One should train in seclusion alone.
As for "seclusion," there are three kinds of seclusion:
Physical seclusion, mental seclusion, and seclusion from acquisitions.
What is physical seclusion? ... [as before] ... This is seclusion from acquisitions.
Physical seclusion belongs to those who dwell in solitude and delight in renunciation;
mental seclusion belongs to those whose minds are purified and who have attained supreme clarity;
and seclusion from acquisitions belongs to persons free from acquisitions who have reached the state beyond conditioned formations.
Training: there are three trainings—
the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom … [as before] … this is the training in higher wisdom.
"One should train in seclusion alone" means: one should train in seclusion, practice it, engage in it thoroughly, and live having undertaken it—one should train in seclusion alone.
"This is the supreme among the noble ones."
The noble ones are said to be the Buddhas, the disciples of the Buddha, and the paccekabuddhas.
Of the noble ones, this is the foremost, the best, the most distinguished, the preeminent, the highest, the most excellent: namely, the practice of seclusion.
This is the supreme among the noble ones.
"One should not think oneself superior because of that.
One should not become conceited through the practice of physical seclusion;

one should not be uplifted, one should not be puffed up, one should not give rise to pride, one should not display strength, one should not display rigidity, one should not generate pride because of that, and one should not be stubborn, haughty, or arrogant.
Therefore, one should not consider oneself superior.
"He is indeed near to Nibbāna" means he is near to, close to, adjacent to, and not far from Nibbāna.
He is indeed close to Nibbāna.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“One should train only in seclusion.”
This is the supreme state of the Noble Ones;
one should not think oneself superior because of it,
for such a person is indeed close to Nibbāna.
They envy the sage who rides on his vehicle,
who wanders without regard for sensual pleasures,
and who has crossed over the flood.
People are infatuated with sensual pleasures, yet the sage wanders empty.
"Empty" means he is empty, secluded, and withdrawn; he is empty, secluded, and withdrawn from bodily misconduct.
By verbal misconduct … [and so on] … by mental misconduct … by lust …
... through hatred ...
through delusion ...
through anger ...
... by malice ...
by hypocrisy ...
by spite ...
... by envy ...
by stinginess ...
by deceit ...
... through deceitfulness ...
through stubbornness ...
through aggression ...
By conceit … by overweening pride … by intoxication …
... by negligence ...
by all defilements ...
by all misconduct ...
...from all distresses ...
from all fevers ...
from all torments ...
Of one who is empty of, secluded from, and withdrawn from all unwholesome volitional formations.
"The sage" (muni): wisdom is called *mona*... [and so on] ...having transcended the snare of attachment, he is a sage.
"Of one who wanders, moves about, dwells, conducts himself, behaves, protects, maintains, and sustains"—
this refers to "the wandering sage who is empty.
"Without regard for sensual pleasures."
Regarding sensual pleasures (*kāma*): in brief, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures—sensual pleasures as objects (*vatthukāma*) and sensual pleasures as defilements (*kilesakāma*).
… [omission] … these are called sensual pleasures as objects. … [omission] …
These are called the defilements of sensual desire (*kilesakāmā*).
Having fully understood the objects of sensual desire (*vatthukāmā*), and having abandoned, relinquished, dispelled, eliminated, and brought to non-existence the defilements of sensual desire,
one looks with indifference toward sensual desires— one who has cast them out, vomited them up, released them, abandoned them, and turned away from them.

One who is free from lust, whose lust has faded, whose lust has been vomited out, whose lust has been transcended, whose lust has been abandoned, whose lust has been relinquished— one who is hungerless,
extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, and who dwells with a self that has become sublime—
such a one is "without regard for sensual pleasures."
Beings who are attached to sensual pleasures long for one who has crossed the flood.

"Beings" is a designation for living creatures; beings who are enamored with, greedy for, attached to, infatuated with, clinging to, stuck to, and fettered by sensual pleasures [long for] one who has crossed the flood of sensuality, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance—the entire path of conditioned formations.
For one who has crossed over, who has emerged, who has gone beyond, who has transcended, who has passed beyond, who has reached the further shore, who has attained the further shore,
who has reached the end, who has attained the end, who has reached the limit, who has attained the limit,
who has reached the boundary, who has attained the boundary, who has reached the final goal, who has attained the final goal, who has reached the refuge, who has attained the refuge.
To one who has attained a shelter, they wish, accept, aspire, yearn, and long for a shelter; to one who has attained a refuge, they wish, accept, aspire, yearn, and long for a refuge;

to one who has attained fearlessness, they wish, accept, aspire, yearn, and long for fearlessness; to one who has attained the undecaying, they wish, accept, aspire, yearn, and long for the undecaying; to one who has attained the deathless, they wish, accept, aspire, yearn, and long for the deathless; to one who has attained Nibbāna, they wish, accept, aspire, yearn, and long for Nibbāna.
Just as debtors long for and desire freedom from debt, just as those who are ill long for and desire health,
just as those bound in fetters long for and desire release from bondage, just as slaves long for and desire freedom,
and just as those set upon a perilous journey through the wilderness long for and desire a land of safety;

In the same way, people who are lustful, greedy, infatuated, obsessed, clinging, stuck, and entangled in sensual pleasures—desire, accept, long for, yearn for, and crave one who has crossed the flood of sensual pleasure, crossed the flood of existence...
[and so on] ...who has reached Nibbāna and attained Nibbāna.
Thus, "people infatuated with sensual pleasures yearn for one who has crossed the flood."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“For the sage who lives empty,
who has no longing for sensual pleasures;”
“People who are obsessed with sensual pleasures long for one who has crossed over the flood.
Thus ends the seventh exposition, the Tissa-Metteyya Sutta.
